title: Humility of the fourth Guru
hook: tradition says Guru Ram Das answered a visitor's question about his beard by wiping the visitor's feet

segments.voice: Yesterday, the city he built: a pool, a bazaar and a sangat side by side in Ramdaspur. Your line was holy in the market. Did you look up at the person behind the counter? Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

Someone you respect comes to visit. A renunciant, famous for his discipline. He looks you up and down and asks, with a small edge to it, why you've let your beard grow so long. A fair question, or a jab? Either way, there are a few easy answers. Explain yourself. Laugh it off. Ask him a question back. Sikh tradition tells a story about Guru Ram Das and exactly that question, and his answer wasn't a word at all. Today: the humility of the fourth Guru.
screen: `A RESPECTED VISITOR.` → `WHY SUCH A LONG BEARD?` → `THE ANSWER ISN'T A WORD.`

segments.voice: The visitor, tradition says, was Baba Sri Chand, the son of Guru Nanak, and a respected ascetic in his own right, honored by the Udasi sadhus. He came to see the fourth Guru and asked about his long beard. Guru Ram Das answered: it's for wiping the feet of holy men like you. And then, the story goes, he knelt and began to do it. Three things make this story land. First, he doesn't defend himself. A question with an edge is usually an invitation to argue. He turns it into an invitation to serve. Second, he serves someone who might have been a rival. Here is the founder's own son, and the Guru who now sits in the founder's place kneels at his feet. The story is told with honor for both men. Third, the story matches his hymns. In a hymn that is part of the Rehras, the Sikh evening prayer, Guru Ram Das speaks to the Guru like this, paraphrased: we are like small worms and insects, O True Guru, and we seek your shelter; be kind, and light up the Name in us. That's not false modesty. It's a Guru who knows that the light he carries isn't his own. Notice how close this sits to the rest of his week. The Guru who asks for the dust of the Gursikh's feet. The Guru who builds a city around a pool for everyone. And the Guru who answers a jab by kneeling. Humble service, in the stories about him, isn't thinking less of yourself. It's being free enough of yourself to kneel.
screen: `BABA SRI CHAND'S QUESTION.` · `TO WIPE THE FEET OF HOLY MEN.` · `WORMS AND INSECTS AT THE GURU'S DOOR.` · `FREE ENOUGH OF YOURSELF TO KNEEL.` · then, large: `HUMILITY OF THE FOURTH GURU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a humble service. In the sit, look over today and find one job nobody wants. The dishes someone else left. Shoes piled at the door. The bathroom. The trash nobody takes out. Choose one. Then picture yourself doing it slowly, without announcing it, without keeping score. Let the breath slow and settle on that picture. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Humility of the fourth Guru. Tradition says that asked about his beard, Guru Ram Das said it was for wiping the feet of holy men, and knelt to do it. Today's word.
screen: `HUMILITY OF THE FOURTH GURU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: humble service. Do the job you chose in the sit, and if someone asks why, you don't have to explain. Day one thousand one hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell this story of Guru Ram Das and Baba Sri Chand when they speak of humility, and seva, humble service such as cleaning shoes and washing dishes at the gurdwara, is part of Sikh community life.

fork.setup: a respected visitor asks, with an edge, why your beard is so long. you're Guru Ram Das. what do you do?
options: say it's for wiping the feet of holy men, and kneel.
ask him why he has none.
fork.reveal: tradition says he answered that way and knelt to wipe the visitor's feet: a jab answered with service.

original.note: humility, the Punjabi word Sikhs use for the lowliness the stories of Guru Ram Das show.

trapdoor: what you thought: humility means thinking little of yourself.
what it means: in the story, being free enough of yourself to kneel, even to a possible rival.
what a scholar hears: 'ham keere kiram satgur sarnaai', Gujri Mahala four, in the evening Rehras.
